speakers: Pablo Calderini (president and CIO, Graham Capital)
summary: Graham Capital 2022 symposium panel on discretionary macro. Argues inflation ended the 2010-20 anomaly of suppressed volatility; central bank divergence, sticky inflation and collapsed stock-bond diversification create opportunity. Heavy emphasis on risk management: vol sizing, shrinking into events, stress tests over VaR.

coverage.note: intro; Fed put and low-inflation reaction function pre-pandemic
transitory call, Fed lag, edge from research, QE to QT
Fed communications, inflation unpredictability, stock-bond correlation, secular changes
risk parity end, QE suppressed vol, bear rallies, 2022 trades
conviction sizing, correlation and VaR vs tails, stress tests
inflation entrenched, terminal rate, European tightening into recession
Japan, Europe winter, QT and real yields
liquidity, sentiment factor, cross-asset correlation at events, investing vs trading

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: the policy priority was really bringing inflation that had been too low for the past decade back up to Target and that very low inflation backdrop had allowed the FED to be quick to ease and slow to tighten
claims.claim: Pre-pandemic, persistently low inflation let the Fed ease quickly and tighten slowly (2015-18 hikes every other meeting at 25bp), creating the fed put and well-telegraphed policy.
claims.testable: partly - reaction function can be estimated by regime

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: the Fed was very confident at that time calling in high inflation transitory because for so long inflation had been so low
claims.claim: The Fed's new average inflation targeting framework (Aug 2020) and its 'transitory' call made it slow to respond to inflation, producing a lag between inflation data and policy that a researcher can exploit.
claims.indicator: Fed policy rate vs inflation prints
claims.direction: Fed behind the curve; short bonds, long USD
claims.conditions: after a long low-inflation period when the Fed is anchored to old regime
claims.testable: partly - lag of Fed vs Taylor-rule gap testable

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: we could come into the Year and have a strong view about where inflation was going where the labor market was going and see that the Fed was really wrongly positioned for this environment
claims.claim: Edge arises when economic research shows the central bank is mispositioned relative to inflation and labour data, since previously telegraphed policy had left little room for such an edge.
claims.indicator: inflation and labour market data vs central bank positioning
claims.testable: partly - compare Taylor-rule gap with market pricing

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: one of the things that I think was so different for Central Bank watching
claims.claim: Central banks worldwide surprised on how aggressive they would be (e.g. 75bp hikes) after a year earlier still doing QE, so the policy debate shifted from taper to pace of tightening.

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: my team doesn't have a house view that PMS have to put on
claims.claim: Process: the economist team provides research and flags where Fed thinking differs from consensus, but portfolio managers express it independently.

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: that they might for example be considering running off their balance
claims.claim: Example of early reading of Fed communications (Dec 2021 press conference hints at earlier balance sheet runoff while still doing QE) as an opportunity outside consensus.
claims.indicator: Fed press conference language; balance sheet runoff timing
claims.direction: short bonds ahead of earlier balance sheet runoff
claims.conditions: when market consensus is not pricing it
claims.testable: partly - text analysis of FOMC communication

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: I think anyone working right now unless they're been working a really long time has never seen inflation like this and when I got into business in the mid 90s used to say inflation was the hardest variable to predict
claims.claim: Inflation is the hardest variable to predict and models built on 20 years of 0.2% monthly prints break down, so central bank response models are unreliable.

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: Global central banks that hike in response to a high headline CPI or even you know the FED height texture in response to a higher than expected Universe University of Michigan uh um inflation expectations survey
claims.claim: Central banks now react to headline CPI and even the Michigan inflation expectations survey, so those releases are tradable policy triggers.
claims.indicator: headline CPI; University of Michigan inflation expectations

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: you have governments that what are they doing they're actually spending more money to help people afford higher prices
claims.claim: Fiscal support for higher prices works against monetary tightening (Back to the Future dynamic), sustaining inflation.

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: the negative correlation between stocks and bonds a lot of people to construct um such uh positive expected value portfolios that's gone
claims.claim: The negative stock-bond correlation underpinning 60/40 portfolios has gone in the inflation regime, so diversification between them fails.
claims.conditions: when inflation is high and central banks hike
claims.testable: yes - rolling stock-bond correlation vs inflation

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: a reversal of the globalization that we've seen for most of our careers um I think a reversal of the capital versus labor Dynamics where labor is developed more power again
claims.claim: Secular changes - deglobalisation and labour regaining power vs capital - support structurally higher inflation.

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: it puts a real premium on maybe risk proper risk management
claims.claim: In a regime where economists and traders are on equal footing with no precedent, premium is on common sense, imagination and risk management.

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: so it's set up risk parity for for decades
claims.claim: Risk parity worked for decades on falling rates and QE tamped volatility, peaking when $7 trillion of debt was negative-yielding and equity valuations at highs; it has since been thrown out.
claims.indicator: risk parity returns; negative-yielding debt stock
claims.conditions: falling-rate low-vol regime; fails when stocks and bonds fall together
claims.testable: yes - risk parity backtest by regime

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: QE brings down Vol and it and it um you know allows people to kind of go well they want the central banks want you to go further out in the risk Spectrum
claims.claim: QE suppresses volatility and pushes investors out the risk spectrum (3% mortgages, cheap credit), whereas withdrawing it raises volatility.
claims.testable: yes - volatility vs balance sheet change

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: there is a fed put but it's it struck so far down that we're not quite sure where that is yet
claims.claim: The Fed put still exists but its strike is far lower because inflation limits easing; buying dips on pivot hopes is the old playbook.

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: the adage is no one makes money in a bear Market because the bear Market rallies are so vicious
claims.claim: Bear markets contain vicious rallies (summer 2022 stocks +20%, 10-year notes rallying 75bp), so a trend-following short must manage sentiment-driven snapbacks.
claims.testable: yes - rally size in bear markets

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: short risk parody which meaning short stocks and short bonds Dollar's been very strong
claims.claim: Most 2022 returns came from short stocks plus short bonds (anti-risk-parity) and long dollar, with extra gains in yen and the Mexican peso (reshoring flows despite carry).
claims.direction: short stocks, short bonds, long USD

claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: this idea of matching conviction two positions and trading dynamically
claims.claim: Macro value comes from scaling positions to conviction, which creates risk-management challenges.

claims.speaker: Chris McCann
claims.quote: in times of the higher correlation we actually have a higher information ratio among our PMS however they also tend to be times of higher volatility
claims.claim: When themes are clear, PM returns correlate more and information ratio is higher, but volatility is higher so position sizes shrink, offsetting risk.

claims.speaker: Chris McCann
claims.quote: tail risks tend to be higher because people have higher position sizes to offset the fact that volatility is low
claims.claim: Low-vol periods give low VaR but larger tail risk because positions are sized up; in high-vol 2022 VaR is high but tails smaller.
claims.testable: yes - tail loss vs vol regime

claims.speaker: Chris McCann
claims.quote: it makes statistics like stress tests more valuable because really that's what we're concerned about in markets like this where Gap risk is really what you need to be concerned about
claims.claim: With unstable correlations VaR loses value; stress tests and gap-risk analysis matter more.

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: the fact that's going down to two is is ludicrous
claims.claim: View: inflation will stay high (or possibly go to deflation) rather than return smoothly to 2%, because the target is arbitrary; liquidity tightening globally is bad for risk assets.

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: we think inflation will mean persistently High
claims.claim: Entrenched services and core goods inflation means the Fed will lift the terminal rate to 4% then 5% and soft landing odds are low.
claims.indicator: core goods and services inflation; terminal rate

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: we're seeing those central banks having to tighten into recessions
claims.claim: European central banks face energy-driven inflation and second-round effects yet must tighten into recession, reversing the fed-put logic of accommodating downside growth risk.

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: there will be really interesting opportunities as perhaps central banks move to easing Cycles
claims.claim: If inflation unexpectedly cooled, easing cycles would also be an opportunity; the team holds both scenarios.

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: defies the imagination that Japan is going to be the only developed country on Earth that doesn't have inflation
claims.claim: Japan's inflation (30-year high at 3%), YCC testing, weak yen and intervention limits create trade opportunities, with BoJ leadership change due.
claims.direction: long inflation in Japan; USDJPY risk
claims.conditions: BoJ must buy JGBs while defending yen

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: the big variable in Europe is is the winner I mean if it's a cold winter
claims.claim: Key variables: European winter weather, China zero-covid policy after party congress.

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: does do real yields keep going because we're uh shrinking our balance sheet larger than we really ever have
claims.claim: Quantitative tightening raises real yields until yields get so high central banks might flinch.
claims.conditions: yields high enough to stress markets

claims.speaker: Chris McCann
claims.quote: they've survived in the markets for a long period of time because they know how to size their positions for for the long run
claims.claim: Risk management structure: frontline PM sizing, a daily risk committee (4000 meetings since GFC), risk team running Greeks, hundreds of shocks and dozens of stress tests, plus qualitative 'why' from the trading floor.

claims.speaker: Chris McCann
claims.quote: I don't say controlling with necessarily the portfolio managers are controlling the risk and we're just advising them
claims.claim: Risk team advises and monitors; PMs own risk, with committee as cold-eyes review.

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: you size or positions and ball units so and and Chris said this earlier you know and higher it falls higher your emotional size is smaller
claims.claim: Size positions in volatility units so higher volatility means smaller positions; prepare for tails and gap risk.

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: liquidity in the markets are terrible and so some trades you just might not take
claims.claim: Poor liquidity means some trades cannot be sized, so illiquid ideas are skipped; place a premium on liquid instruments.

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: there is a factor that's I would call a sentiment Factor so sometimes things get correlated everything that's overbought gets sold and everything that's open
claims.claim: A sentiment factor: everything overbought gets sold and oversold gets bought, correlating positions; PMs monitor this.

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: these things will all be one trade so the idea of shrinking the book
claims.claim: Across asset classes dollar, rates and equities become one trade into central bank meetings, so book size is shrunk to avoid a triple-sized bet.
claims.conditions: correlations near one around central bank meetings

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: there's investing in trading and you can do both so you have your themes your have your core views
claims.claim: Combine core thematic positions with trading around them (add on retraces, press squeezes, fade, take profits at key levels).

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: what positions are too big and what positions are too small
claims.claim: Daily team risk meeting asks which positions are too big or too small.

claims.speaker: Chris McCann
claims.quote: portfolio managers especially this year where there are a lot of opportunities to react have been tending to scale down into events and then reacting to what happens
claims.claim: With no edge on any given event, scale down into events and react afterwards, using liquidity to rescale (unlike long-only or illiquid books).

claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: I think it's time that we start seeing the 2010-20 period as an anomaly
claims.claim: Pre-2010 volatility was the norm; the 2010-20 suppressed-vol era (easing met every shock) was an anomaly, so expect higher volatility ahead and inflation requires tighter policy responses.
